643:   bytes), and the file goes back to re-requestable (STALLED) with a mismatch count. The next REQUEST, with
644:   coverage ending at the bad block, asks the same device first (a holder checks blocks as it reads, §9, so a
645:   rotten copy stops at the source), then the candidate order continues. After `fileHashRetryLimit` mismatches
646:   the file is FAILED.
647: - **Progress ACKs** (coverage in the transfer's own chunk indices, capped, §3.2) flow back to each transfer's
648:   pusher.
649: - **The gap trigger.** If P does not advance for `fileStallTimeout` (minutes — deliberately beyond the
650:   sender's `chunkAckTimeout` so the push machinery acts first), the
651:   file goes STALLED — re-requestable, not refused — the durable coverage is kept, and the REQUEST path re-opens
652:   with held coverage (§9). **It cancels nothing.** The live incoming transfers stay: byte coverage merges
653:   whatever arrives from whichever source, a transfer that is really dead ends by its TTL, and a serve from a
654:   device that was already pushing supersedes that push at the serving device (§9). Cancelling would throw away
655:   the one copy that needs no holder online: a receiver that was offline for a few minutes while a relay was
656:   forwarding would come back, cancel, answer the relay's next chunk DECLINED and make it drop a whole copy —
657:   the opposite of §7's "the receiver needs no stall detection on relay pushes". The timer counts only while
658:   this device is running, so waking from sleep does not fire it at once. On a large fetch, where a dead source
659:   cannot be superseded, it ends the fetch with an `ABORT` (§6.6). TTL
660:   expiry is the passive backstop; the trigger is the active path.
661: - **Restart.** P is the persisted `contiguous_bytes`; at open the `.part` is truncated to it (a torn or
662:   uncommitted append is cut away, and the staged rows it came from are still there to drain again), and the
663:   partial block at P is re-hashed. Staged ranges rehydrate from their table; missing is the complement of
664:   durable coverage. What was ACKed was durable, so nothing ACKed is ever lost.
665: 
666: ## 9. The pull path: REQUEST
667: 
668: The recovery mechanism for everything the push path failed to deliver, and the only way history-acquired
669: files get their bytes.
670: 
671: - **Trigger** (orchestrator inbound pipeline, on message ingest — the message may have arrived by push or by
672:   sync): a message references a `fileId` with no completed local file and no progressing transfer. Guards:
673:     - **large files: the device's decision** — at or below `autoDownloadMaxBytes` the trigger fires at once (nothing is
674:       pushed, so there is nothing to wait for); above it, only a user click fires it (§8);
675:     - small files: a grace period before the first attempt (`fileRequestFirstAttemptDelay`) — the OFFER may be in
676:       flight, or
677:     may never come (the sibling case, §2); the grace period is the only thing telling "late" and "never"
678:     apart, and it errs on the quiet side;
679:     - **STALLED / EXPIRED are re-requestable** (something broke; try again — a hash mismatch below the retry
680:       limit lands here too, §8); **DECLINED / CANCELLED / FAILED are refused** — never auto-resurrect a file the
681:       user declined or that exhausted its retries; those need a user re-open;
682:   - dedup by `fileId` (message duplicates create one row).
683: - **One candidate at a time, never parallel** — parallel asks would make N devices each serve the entire
684:   file; that is the spam/DDoS shape. Candidates: the sender's devices, then own-account siblings (room
685:   members later), link-availability filtered like sync.
686: - **The attempt is sync-shaped: the REQUEST is ACKed ("I hold it, serving") or NACKed DECLINED ("I don't, or
687:   I won't") — and the OFFER is the reply**, exactly like a sync request's ACK-then-reply. On ACK the request
688:   waits (WAITING) with a timeout for the OFFER; on timeout or DECLINED the next candidate is asked at once.
689:   All candidates declined → "file unavailable" (terminal; a new sync or a user re-open retries).
690: - **A large request is a fetch, not a REQUEST envelope** (§6.6). The same loop picks the candidate; the
691:   attempt then opens a session and a fetch channel instead of enqueueing a packet, `FETCH_OK` plays the ACK
692:   and `FETCH_DECLINED` the DECLINED, and there is no WAITING state because the answer and the bytes come on
693:   the same channel. A candidate that cannot be
694:   reached is not a decline: when every remaining candidate is merely unreachable, the request stays PENDING and
695:   retries when one of them comes online — for WebRTC-only bytes, offline holders are the normal case. A
696:   candidate that is online but cannot be connected to is recorded as "no direct connection" so the GUI can say
697:   so (§6.6). A fetch that ends with its session sends the request back to PENDING, asking the same candidate
698:   first.
699: - The small-file REQUEST is **ratchet-sealed** (it carries the `fileId`) and **direct-only** (§3.2). It carries **held
700:   coverage** in bytes (`contiguousBytes` + missing ranges, capped; heavy fragmentation degrades to
701:   contiguous-only — a coarser serve with more duplicates, still correct).
702: - **The serve gate — the same logic as sync's.** A holder serves only when the requesting account may see a
703:   message that references the `fileId`: the orchestrator's `message_attachments` index (filled at DAG ingest)
704:   maps the `fileId` to its messages, and the sync serve gate decides visibility of those messages. No visible
705:   referencing message → DECLINED. Without the gate, anyone who has or guesses a file's content could pull it
706:   from any holder by its hash. A large fetch passes the same gate before `FETCH_OK`: the requesting account
707:   is the account of the session's peer device.
708: - **Holders check blocks as they read.** AEAD only protects bytes in transit: a copy that rotted on disk, or a
709:   referenced original the user edited (§10), would be encrypted faithfully and fail only at the requester. So
710:   the plaintext source hashes each block it reads and compares it with the block list before the block's bytes go
711:   out (a serve that starts mid-block reads from that block's start) — no full re-hash before a serve, which at
712:   100 GB would take minutes every time. A mismatch or a missing
713:   file ends the transfer with a CANCEL (a fetch with an `ABORT`); the holder treats the file as not held (a reference
714:   becomes
715:   SOURCE_LOST, §10) and DECLINEs later REQUESTs for it.
716: - For a small file, the serving device (any holder: original sender, sibling that completed) re-runs the push engine
717:   with a **fresh
718:   `transferId` and a fresh key**, covering the suffix from the floor-aligned boundary at or below the
719:   requester's lowest missing byte (§3.4). Mixed chunkings are correct — the receiver is param-agnostic.
720: - **One live transfer per (`fileId`, target device) at a serving device.** A REQUEST that reaches a device
721:   already pushing that file to the requester (a late OFFER after the grace period, a stalled push) supersedes
722:   it: the old transfer is CANCELled and the serve starts fresh from the held coverage. Never two parallel
723:   transfers of one file from one device to one device.
724: - The candidate-asking loop is **extracted as a shared core with `SyncRetryProcessor`** (the needs now
725:   coincide; on success the file request hands off to the transfer engine instead of consuming a reply payload
726:   — a callback seam, not a structural fork).
727: - Relays are **not** candidates: they are transient push caches with forget-after-delivery semantics.
728: 
729: ## 10. Storage and retention
730: 
731: - **Sender/holder: the GUI picks, the core does the rest.** The GUI owns only the platform file chooser and a **"keep a
732:   copy" checkbox**, checked by default at or below `copyIntoStoreMaxBytes` (default
733:   `smallFileMaxBytes`) and unchecked above it. The orchestrator's send API takes the choice:
734:     - **Copy** — the file is copied into **app-internal storage** before anything is sent, hashed in the same
735:       pass. The source is immutable across restarts, and a picture survives the user clearing their
736:       downloads folder. A few MB of extra space is worth that for memes and photos.
737:     - **Reference** — the descriptor records the original's path (on Android a persistable URI permission) and
738:       the file is hashed in place. Nothing is duplicated, which matters at 100 GB. The store does not own it: it
739:       is outside the quota and never deleted by retention. If the original is moved, deleted or edited, the
740:       block check while serving catches it (§9) and the descriptor goes SOURCE_LOST: this device stops serving
741:       it, the message still shows the attachment, and other holders may still serve it.
742: 
743:   Either way the orchestrator owns the store's directory layout, retention and quota, **vending paths and
744:   metadata to the GUI** for rendering; the GUI never writes into the store. Hashing 100 GB takes minutes; the
745:   message is published once the `fileId` is known, and the GUI shows the attachment as preparing until then. **Keep
746:   forever** is the default policy — serverlessness
747:   forces it (the bytes are on a device or nowhere; there is no lazy-loading when a user scrolls back a year).
748:   Knob: per-account quota with LRU above it. A file the quota evicts goes `EVICTED`: its descriptor is
749:   removed, this device stops serving it, the message still shows the attachment, and it is fetched again only
750:   when the user opens it — never automatically, or the quota would evict and re-fetch in a loop.
751: - **Receiver**: the same permanent store once READY; `.part` until verified.
752: - **Relay**: transient ciphertext only — pledged-storage-capped (§15), TTL'd, forget-after-delivery.
753: - **Transfers are temporary; files stay** (§1). v1 has no bare transfers — every transfer belongs to a
754:   message-composed send; a GUI-only send without a message, if it ever exists, gets its own table (§18).
755: 
756: ## 11. File I/O: kotlinx.io plus one positioned read
757: 
758: kotlinx.io is the house standard already (`ConfigStore`, `JvmAppLogger`, `KmpTorBackend`, `DataDirLock`,
759: `Platform`), and v1 uses it everywhere but one place — positioned I/O is on kotlinx.io's roadmap (files-API
760: redesign, kotlinx-io issue #241) but not shipped, so the design needs it only for reads:
761: 
762: - **The receiver is a single append-only writer position** (P, §8): staged ranges absorb arbitrary arrival
763:   order and mixed chunkings, so the writer never seeks — small and large alike. A staged range's tail beyond P is
764:   sliced in memory at drain; block verification hashes the bytes as they are appended.
765: - **The sender reads at an offset — the one exception to pure kotlinx.io.** Every large fetch starts at the
766:   requester's P (§6.6), and every session drop starts a new fetch, so skipping by reading through the prefix
767:   would re-read up to the whole file each time. The I/O module therefore has a **positioned read**
768:   (`expect`/`actual` over `FileChannel` on JVM and Android) behind its chunk-shaped boundary; reads stay linear
769:   from the start offset.
770: - A torn append (crash mid-drain) is truncated at open to the persisted P (§8) — the DB is the checkpoint,
771:   the file length never is.
772: - The chunk-shaped I/O boundary (`readChunk`/`writeChunk`-style module) still exists as a module, with a
773:   kotlinx.io implementation inside apart from the positioned read — so when #241 ships positioned I/O, the
774:   swap is internal, not a design change.

776: ## 12. Layering and data ownership
777: 
778: **Two grains, one seam:**
779: 
780: - **Routing owns the `transferId` grain** — device vocabulary: the per-device fan-out, per-transfer chunk
781:   parameters, per-depot resume points (the pusher's state, restart-recoverable from its rows plus the
782:   outbox), the incoming-transfer rows, chunk encryption and decryption, sealed-half protection and every transfer key,
783:   **all
784:   transfer signaling** — OFFER, CHUNK, ACK, COMPLETE and CANCEL travel between the two devices that
785:   participate in the transfer — the relay store, and the request attempts. For large files it owns the fetch
786:   channel (§6.6): opening the session and the channel, the frames, the credit window — device and channel
787:   vocabulary, with no table.
788: - **The orchestrator owns the `fileId`/account grain** — file vocabulary: send rows per (file, peer account),
789:   receive state per `fileId` (coverage, checkpoints, block verification), serve rows per (file, requester
790:   account), the serve gate, the accept/decline verdicts (including the large-file auto-download decision),
791:   the store's copies and references, and the REQUEST trigger. It never holds a key. It sees account-level events through
792:   the `FileCarrier` port and issues
793:   account-level ops; source devices may appear in events as *facts* (like "re-verify messages from a
794:   device"), never as *addresses* — replies are routing-owned signaling.
795: 
796: The precedent is the message path: the router fans out per device and the orchestrator never addresses one;
797: files push the same line one step further (transfer state itself is device-grain, so it lives routing-side).
798: A headless relay node's orchestrator (file service, REQUEST logic, GUI progress) is completely uninvolved in
799: forwarding. Serve-on-REQUEST is the one relay-node case that *is* orchestrator business (we hold the file →
800: own traffic → our row, account-grain, pushed through the same machinery).
801:

902: ## 14. State machines
903: 
904: See [`transfer states.mmd`](transfer%20states.mmd). Compact listing:
905: 
906: - **Sender transfer (per device, routing)**: CREATED → IN_FLIGHT (offer accepted) → COMPLETED (COMPLETE from
907:   the target; deposits cancelled) / **ENDED** (outcome unknown: a target's DECLINED on a chunk — the transfer
908:   is gone there, §3.6 — or another terminal NACK on the marker, §6.1; never shown as delivered) /
909:   EXPIRED (`fileTransferTtl`) / **DECLINED (the target declined the OFFER — terminal for this device)** /
910:   CANCELLED (user cancel, or superseded by a serve to the same device, §9).
911: - **Fetch (large, routing, in memory only)**: ASKED (channel open, `FETCH` sent) → STREAMING (`FETCH_OK`,
912:   block list checked) → done (READY, channel closed) / ended (`FETCH_DECLINED`, session or channel dropped,
913:   `ABORT` from the receiver's gap trigger, or a block mismatch at the source). No row on either end: an ended
914:   fetch is forgotten, and the next one starts from the checkpointed P.
915: - **Incoming transfer (`transferId`-scoped, routing)**: ACTIVE (OFFER processed) → dropped on COMPLETE sent,
916:   CANCEL either way, or expiry. The gap trigger does not end it (§8).
917: - **Receiver (`fileId`-scoped)**: PENDING → IN_FLIGHT (`.part` reserved) → READY (coverage complete, last
918:   block verified, renamed, COMPLETE to live authors); IN_FLIGHT → STALLED on a block mismatch below
919:   `fileHashRetryLimit` (`.part` truncated to the block's start), FAILED at the limit; IN_FLIGHT → FAILED (ENOSPC);
920:   PENDING → DECLINED (no space, or a large file this device did not fetch — local, re-openable by
921:   the user); IN_FLIGHT → **STALLED** (no prefix progress within `fileStallTimeout` → REQUEST re-opens; live
922:   transfers are left alone); STALLED → IN_FLIGHT when any source resumes delivery; READY → **EVICTED** (quota
923:   LRU; fetched again only on a user re-open); IN_FLIGHT that never progresses expires → the REQUEST
924:   trigger re-opens.
925: - **Relay transfer**: RESERVED (admitted) → WHOLE (covered suffix complete) → FORWARDING (offer ACKed) →
926:   DRAINED; EXPIRED (reservation TTL or transfer TTL) from RESERVED/WHOLE; **dropped when the target DECLINED
927:   the forwarded OFFER**.
928: - **Request**: PENDING → ASKING (one candidate; a large request first opens a session) → **WAITING (ACK;
929:   offer pending, timeout → next candidate)** → SATISFIED (OFFER received; the serve transfer takes over) /
930:   UNAVAILABLE (every candidate declined or expired). A large request whose remaining candidates are only
931:   unreachable stays PENDING until one comes online. A large request has no WAITING: ASKING → SATISFIED on
932:   `FETCH_OK`, and SATISFIED → PENDING when the fetch ends with its session.
933: - **Marker** (outbox row): unchanged from the message contract — QUEUED → dispatched → gone on ACK / terminal
934:   NACK / expiry; retries resume, never restart. Only a target's DECLINED is a refusal; other terminal NACKs
935:   end the transfer as ENDED (§6.1).

975: ## 16. Invariants
976: 
977: 1. Anything a relay pushes is whole — count-based check over the covered suffix; this is the ceiling by
978:    design (the relay cannot and must not verify content).
979: 2. One relay hop, ever: deposits happen only at a transfer's authoring device (a serve is an authoring
980:    device too), redundancy is parallel (same covered set at every policy-selected relay), forwarding relays
981:    never re-deposit, the sender never chases a failing relay.
982: 3. Relays are not REQUEST candidates; relays forget after delivery.
983: 4. Never READY without full byte coverage and every block verified; P is never committed past an unverified
984:    block. A mismatch is a failed attempt costing one block, retried a bounded number of times.
985: 5. A transfer's key travels only inside its OFFER's ratchet-sealed half — never in messages, never in the
986:    clear — and lives no longer than its transfer. Only routing and protection ever hold one.
987: 6. Key and chunk parameters are per transfer; chunk AEAD binds (`transferId`, `chunkIndex`) as AAD. Nothing
988:    relies on ciphertext being reproducible.
989: 7. Covered sets are contiguous suffixes in the transfer's own chunking; per-depot engine state is one resume
990:    point.
991: 8. The marker is establishment-only; ACK = processed: an outbox chunk is processed when decrypted and durably
992:    staged; a fetch's `PROGRESS` is sent only after the fsync and the P commit (§8).
993: 9. Receiver file state is `fileId`-scoped byte coverage — transfer- and chunking-agnostic; each incoming
994:    transfer is its own `transferId`-scoped row; relay state is `transferId`-scoped.
995: 10. One REQUEST candidate at a time.
996: 11. STALLED / EXPIRED are re-requestable; DECLINED / CANCELLED / FAILED / EVICTED are refused — never
997:     auto-resurrected. The gap trigger opens a REQUEST and cancels no transfer.
998: 12. The relay verifies the original sender's signature on OFFER and CHUNK before storing anything; chunks
999:     without a live transfer row are DECLINED at the door, never stored.
1000: 13. Transfers are temporary (`fileTransferTtl`); files stay.
1001: 14. A transfer's chunks flow only after its OFFER was processed by the target (§3.5).
1002: 15. Any DECLINED touching a transfer cleans up that party's state for it; only the target's DECLINED **on an
1003:     OFFER** is terminal for the send to that device — a DECLINED on a chunk ends the transfer quietly as
1004:     ENDED (§3.6). A sender transfer is COMPLETED only by a COMPLETE.
1005: 16. Transfers are device-to-device; the orchestrator speaks files and accounts, routing fans out and signals
1006:     per device.
1007: 17. In envelopes the `fileId` travels only in the OFFER's sealed half and the sealed, direct-only REQUEST;
1008:     every other FILE envelope is addressed by `transferId`. Outside envelopes it appears only in a fetch's
1009:     `FETCH` frame, inside the DTLS channel to the one peer device.
1010: 18. Every serve passes the serve gate: the requester's account must see a message referencing the `fileId`.
1011: 19. One sealed OFFER per transfer, and one transfer per relay deposit; at a serving device, one live transfer
1012:     per (`fileId`, target device).
1013: 20. Large files are pull-only: nothing large is sent unasked; the receiving device decides to fetch, and
1014:     declining is local. `smallFileMaxBytes` is one value for the whole network.
1015: 21. A fetch lives within one data channel of one WebRTC session; it never waits for a session and never goes
1016:     over Tor, a relay, the outbox or the envelope pipeline.
1017: 22. The `fileId` is computed by one protocol-fixed rule (§2); a block list is used only after it hashes to the
1018:     `fileId`, and a holder sends no block it has not just checked against the list.
1019: 23. A fetch's bytes are protected by the channel alone (DTLS, authenticated through signed and sealed
1020:     signaling, §4). If WebRTC signaling ever stops being signed and sealed to the peer device, the fetch needs
1021:     its own encryption before that ships.
1022: 24. Chunk rows deposit only on signals that the target is gone (link closed, no link, no chunk ACK at all
1023:     within `chunkAckTimeout`) — never on one slow or retried chunk (§6.3).
1024: 25. A received file that no message references within `fileTransferTtl` is deleted (§8).

1026: ## 17. Rejected alternatives
1027: 
1028: Recorded so they are not relitigated:
1029: 
1030: - **Whole file as one packet** — transport frame caps (250 KiB WebRTC, 4 MB Tor) make it impossible; chunking
1031:   everywhere.
1032: - **Chunk content through the Double Ratchet** — ratchet state explosion, `MAX_SKIP` bounds, chain breakage
1033:   for interleaved messages; a per-transfer symmetric key instead.
1034: - **A key in the message plaintext** — transfers must be self-contained; the OFFER's sealed half is the
1035:   single key carrier (§3.3).
1036: - **One key per file with deterministic per-range ciphertext** — the original design: it needed range-derived
1037:   nonces to avoid nonce reuse across chunkings, keys stored with the file and re-sealed on every serve, and
1038:   broke outright when two senders of the same file generated two keys. Cross-holder ciphertext identity
1039:   bought nothing the receiver's plaintext coverage doesn't already give; per-transfer keys instead (§4).
1040: - **`fileId`-keyed control packets** — ACKs to a forwarding relay would hand it the plaintext hash; control
1041:   packets are addressed by `transferId` (§3.2).
1042: - **Keeping incoming-transfer rows to answer late chunks** — any retention window can be outlived by one more
1043:   late packet (the two generals); rows die with their transfer and a late chunk ends the transfer quietly (§3.6).
1044: - **Relay-held chunks as outbox `is_relay` rows** — the relay cache budget is shared with messages (one 10 MB
1045:   file would consume it entirely), per-row LRU eviction strands transfers, and making it safe would push
1046:   transfer-awareness into the most battle-tested component. Dedicated tables isolate it.
1047: - **Relay chunks on disk** — at ≤10 MB the DB gives transactional admission/eviction/crash recovery for free.
1048: - **Marker held open until transfer completion** — needs a "processed but don't ACK" result, fights every
1049:   message-scale outbox assumption, and duplicates state the engine owns.
1050: - **Parallel REQUEST fan-out** — N devices each serving the entire file is the spam shape; one candidate at a
1051:   time.
1052: - **Relays as REQUEST candidates** — simplified away; relays are pure push caches.
1053: - **Eager per-chunk relay forwarding** — gate on wholeness instead: the latency cost is theoretical (the relay
1054:   path is only used when the direct path already failed), and the invariant "a relay push is always whole" is
1055:   worth more.
1056: - **Sparse covered sets** — the suffix invariant (§3.4) covers every case with bounded duplicate re-sends and
1057:   one number of per-depot state.
1058: - **Sequential relay re-deposit (chasing)** — spreads the file across the network; one jump.
1059: - **Media tracks (RTP/SRTP) for file streaming** — real-time and lossy by design; files need the data
1060:   channel's reliability.
1061: - **App-layer AEAD, envelopes and per-chunk signatures on the large path** — the earlier design, kept "for
1062:   uniformity with the relay path". Once large files became pull-only and WebRTC-only there was no relay path
1063:   to be uniform with: the bytes cross one authenticated, encrypted channel, and the block list is the
1064:   integrity check. A plain fetch protocol on the channel removes the key, the OFFER, the `transferId`, two
1065:   routing rows and the question of how its control packets get ACKed (§6.6).
1066: - **A large-file fallback to Tor when WebRTC cannot connect** — 100 MB and up over onion circuits is not a
1067:   path worth having; the failure is shown to the user instead (§6.6).
1068: - **A per-device `smallFileMaxBytes`** — requester and holder must agree on the class; it is a network value (§1).
1069: - **A second payload type, or an optional trailing block, for attachments** — a patch to keep old bytes
1070:   decoding while nothing deployed needs them; the layout is changed plainly and the version bumped (§3.1).
1071: - **Message-style deposit triggers on every chunk row** — one slow ACK or one retry would send the remainder
1072:   to every relay on a slow but working link (§6.3).
1073: - **The gap trigger cancelling live transfers** — it would make a returning receiver drop a relay's whole
1074:   copy; coverage merges, so nothing needs cancelling (§8).
1075: - **Showing a transfer as COMPLETED when a chunk is DECLINED** — the transfer is gone at the target, which
1076:   may equally mean it stalled or expired there; that outcome is ENDED (§3.6).
1077: - **Receiver-side chunk-parameter enforcement** — byte coverage (§8) makes mixed chunkings contribute instead
1078:   of conflict; rejecting useful data on principle buys nothing (the block hashes are the gate). Chunk parameters
1079:   are snapshotted per transfer and never compared across transfers.
1080: - **One staging table for relay and receive** — one owner per table (guide §4), and ciphertext for foreign
1081:   traffic never mixes with own plaintext; the two stores share a shape, never a table (§13).
1082: - **The OFFER as the REQUEST's ACK** — outbox rows must leave through their own disposition, not an
1083:   out-of-band correlation; the request is ACKed and the OFFER follows, exactly like sync (§9).
1084: - **Unbounded receive staging** — a racing transfer can stage a whole suffix behind a stuck gap; the
1085:   `maxStagedBytes` bound plus DEFER backpressure closes it (§8).
1086: - **Positioned writes in v1** — the receiver keeps a single append position and staged ranges. Only reads are
1087:   positioned (§11), because a large fetch starts at an offset after every session drop; swap in kotlinx.io
1088:   positioned I/O when it ships (#241).
1089: - **Pushed large OFFERs with an accept prompt** — the original large-path outline: an OFFER held processed
1090:   while the user decides, a separate accept signal, a rule for which devices prompt, a sender waiting for a
1091:   session, and timers that must not fire meanwhile. Pull-only removes all of it (§5, §6.6).
1092: - **Per-chunk ACKs and outbox rows on the large path** — about 475k rows for 100 GB on a channel that already
1093:   delivers in order; `PROGRESS` at checkpoints with a credit window instead (§6.6).
1094: - **Relying on the channel's flow control alone** — `bufferedAmount` protects only the sender; the receive
1095:   callback has no backpressure, so a slow disk would buffer in memory. The credit window bounds it (§6.6).
1096: - **A fetch that waits for its session** — it would need state at both ends and a waiting state; a new fetch
1097:   from the checkpointed P is the same result with no state at all.
1098: - **A plain whole-file SHA-256 `fileId`** — a mismatch throws away the whole file, verification is one more
1099:   full pass at the end and cannot resume after a restart, and every serve needs a full re-hash first. The
1100:   block-hashed `fileId` fixes all three (§2).
1101: - **A Merkle tree with per-chunk proofs** — finer than needed: blocks capped at 1024 per file keep the list at
1102:   32 KiB, small enough to send whole in every OFFER.
1103: - **One fsync per chunk** — ~230 a second at 50 MB/s; checkpoints batch them (§8).
1104: - **Always copying into the store** — doubles 100 GB on disk; the user picks copy or reference (§10).

1129: ## 19. Test matrix
1130: 
1131: - Small file, target offline: deposit → wholeness → forward on surfacing → verify → READY.
1132: - Mid-transfer restarts: sender restart mid-push (resumes from outbox rows); relay restart mid-forward (free
1133:   recovery); receiver restart mid-assembly (staging + prefix re-derivation — nothing ACKed is ever lost).
1134: - Concurrent mixed-chunking transfers: two transfers with different chunk parameters interleave on one file;
1135:   byte coverage completes; hash verifies; COMPLETE reaches both authors.
1136: - Direct-link break mid-send: remainder deposit at the policy-selected relays; holes below the prefix are
1137:   inside the remainder; target completes from direct prefix + relay remainder.
1138: - Duplicate relay forwards: target drops fully-covered ranges; second relay drains on duplicate ACKs.
1139: - Stall → immediate deposit; sender killed right after → relays hold a whole copy.
1140: - Gap trigger: prefix stalls beyond `fileStallTimeout` → STALLED → REQUEST → serve from the lowest missing
1141:   byte; the stalled transfers are not cancelled.
1142: - Staging bound: a racing transfer hits `maxStagedBytes` → DEFER backpressure → gap filled → drain → resume.
1143: - Eviction pressure → DECLINED at admission → engine tries the next relay / re-offers later.
1144: - Chunks for a dead, evicted or expired `transferId` at a relay → DECLINED at the door → sender cleans that
1145:   depot.
1146: - Target declines the relay-forwarded OFFER (no space) → relay drops the transfer, frees quota.
1147: - Sender dies mid-deposit: partial never pushed; reservation TTL cleans; target's REQUEST recovers from a
1148:   holder.
1149: - Large file, auto-download: the message lands → the requester opens a session and a fetch channel → `FETCH`
1150:   → `FETCH_OK` → `DATA` → READY; nothing goes over Tor, a relay or the outbox.
1151: - Large file above `autoDownloadMaxBytes`: no fetch until the user clicks; declining sends nothing; a
1152:   re-open later fetches it.
1153: - Fetch session drops mid-file: both ends forget it → request PENDING → a new fetch starts at the checkpointed
1154:   P with a positioned read; same for a restart on either side.
1155: - `FETCH_OK` with a block list that does not hash to the `fileId` → channel closed, nothing written, next
1156:   candidate.
1157: - Fetch serve gate: a `FETCH` from a device whose account sees no referencing message gets `FETCH_DECLINED`.
1158: - A REQUEST envelope for a file above `smallFileMaxBytes` is DECLINED.
1159: - No direct connection: the holder is online over Tor but no session forms → recorded as such, not as
1160:   offline, and no byte goes over Tor.
1161: - Deposit triggers: a slow link that still ACKs a chunk within `chunkAckTimeout` never deposits; a closed link
1162:   deposits at once; a silent dead link deposits after one timeout.
1163: - Gap trigger keeps transfers: receiver offline mid-forward beyond `fileStallTimeout`, back online → the
1164:   relay's forward continues and completes; the REQUEST that opened is satisfied or superseded.
1165: - Messages first: a text message enqueued behind a full chunk window to the same peer is sent before the
1166:   remaining chunks.
1167: - Chunk DEFER: a chunk DEFERred at the staging bound keeps retrying at `fileChunkRetryDelay` and lands once P
1168:   advances — no hour-long standby.
1169: - Marker terminal NACK other than DECLINED → the transfer is ENDED, never shown as declined or delivered.

package org.yapyap.orchestrator.file.io

import kotlinx.io.Source
import kotlinx.io.files.Path

/**
 * Chunk-shaped I/O boundary (design §11).
 *
 * The receiver is a single append-only writer position; the sender reads at an
 * offset. Only reads are positioned — the writer never seeks.
 */
internal interface AppendHandle : AutoCloseable {
    fun write(bytes: ByteArray, offset: Int = 0, length: Int = bytes.size - offset)
    fun flushAndSync()
    fun truncate(length: Long)
    fun size(): Long
}

internal interface PositionedHandle : AutoCloseable {
    fun size(): Long
    fun readAt(offset: Long, buf: ByteArray, bufOffset: Int, length: Int): Int
}

/**
 * Platform file access, declared by the orchestrator and supplied by `Platform`.
 *
 * Regular `Path` files use the app's data directory. Content URIs (`content://…`)
 * exist only on Android, where the core cannot open them alone — the platform
 * implementation bridges to `ContentResolver`. On JVM both content methods
 * return null; on iOS content URIs do not occur.
 *
 * The orchestrator never imports `wiring` (guide §3): the composition root
 * connects this port to `Platform`.
 */
internal interface FileAccess {
    fun exists(path: Path): Boolean
    fun createDirectories(path: Path)
    fun fileSize(path: Path): Long?
    fun freeSpaceBytes(directory: Path): Long
    fun openAppendWriter(path: Path, truncateToLength: Long?): AppendHandle
    fun openPositionedReader(path: Path, startOffset: Long = 0): PositionedHandle
    suspend fun contentSize(uri: String): Long?
    fun openContentSource(uri: String): Source?
    fun openContentPositionedReader(uri: String, startOffset: Long = 0): PositionedHandle?
}

package org.yapyap.orchestrator.file

import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest
import kotlinx.io.files.Path
import kotlinx.io.files.SystemTemporaryDirectory
import org.yapyap.crypto.primitives.DefaultCryptoProvider
import org.yapyap.orchestrator.file.io.AppendHandle
import org.yapyap.orchestrator.file.io.FileAccess
import org.yapyap.orchestrator.file.io.JvmFileAccess
import org.yapyap.orchestrator.file.io.PositionedHandle
import org.yapyap.persistence.openMemoryDatabase
import org.yapyap.protocol.blockSizeFor
import org.yapyap.routing.file.FileReadResult
import kotlin.test.Test
import kotlin.test.assertContentEquals
import kotlin.test.assertEquals
import kotlin.test.assertTrue
import kotlin.time.Clock
import kotlin.uuid.Uuid

/** Records the lowest absolute offset ever read: proves prefix-skipping. */
private class RecordingAccess(private val delegate: FileAccess = JvmFileAccess()) : FileAccess by delegate {
    var minReadOffset: Long = Long.MAX_VALUE
        private set
    var readCalls: Long = 0
        private set

    override fun openPositionedReader(path: Path, startOffset: Long): PositionedHandle {
        val inner = delegate.openPositionedReader(path, startOffset)
        return object : PositionedHandle {
            override fun size(): Long = inner.size()
            override fun readAt(offset: Long, buf: ByteArray, bufOffset: Int, length: Int): Int {
                readCalls++
                val absolute = startOffset + offset
                if (absolute < minReadOffset) minReadOffset = absolute
                return inner.readAt(offset, buf, bufOffset, length)
            }

            override fun close() = inner.close()
        }
    }

    override fun openAppendWriter(path: Path, truncateToLength: Long?): AppendHandle =
        delegate.openAppendWriter(path, truncateToLength)
}

class FilePlaintextSourceJvmTest {
    private val crypto = DefaultCryptoProvider()

    private fun tempDir(prefix: String): Path {
        val access = JvmFileAccess()
        val dir = Path(SystemTemporaryDirectory.toString(), "$prefix-${Uuid.random()}")
        access.createDirectories(dir)
        return dir
    }

    @Test
    fun serve_startingMidBlock_returnsExactSlice() = runTest {
        val db = openMemoryDatabase().database
        val access = JvmFileAccess()
        val work = tempDir("yapyap-plaintext-mid")
        val storeDir = Path(work.toString(), "store")
        val descriptors = DefaultFileDescriptorStore(db)
        val store = DefaultFileStore(descriptors, crypto, access, storeDir, FileServiceConfig(), Clock.System)
        val bytes = ByteArray(3_000_000) { (it % 251).toByte() }
        val src = Path(work.toString(), "mid.bin")
        access.openAppendWriter(src, null).use {
            it.write(bytes)
            it.flushAndSync()
        }
        val descriptor = store.import(FileImportSource.PathSource(src), "mid.bin", null, keepCopy = true)
        val source = DefaultFilePlaintextSource(descriptors, access, crypto)
        // 1 MiB blocks here; start inside block 1 and span into block 2.
        val offset = 1_000_000L
        val res = source.read(descriptor.fileId, offset, 600_000)
        check(res is FileReadResult.Ok)
        assertEquals(600_000, res.bytes.size)
        assertContentEquals(bytes.copyOfRange(offset.toInt(), offset.toInt() + 600_000), res.bytes)
    }

    @Test
    fun rottenBlock_stopsAtBlock_andMarksDescriptor() = runTest {
        val db = openMemoryDatabase().database
        val access = JvmFileAccess()
        val work = tempDir("yapyap-plaintext-rot")
        val storeDir = Path(work.toString(), "store")
        val descriptors = DefaultFileDescriptorStore(db)
        val store = DefaultFileStore(descriptors, crypto, access, storeDir, FileServiceConfig(), Clock.System)
        val bytes = ByteArray(3_000_000) { (it * 3).toByte() }
        val src = Path(work.toString(), "rot.bin")
        access.openAppendWriter(src, null).use {
            it.write(bytes)
            it.flushAndSync()
        }
        val descriptor = store.import(FileImportSource.PathSource(src), "rot.bin", null, keepCopy = true)
        // Rot the stored copy inside block 1.
        val stored = Path(descriptor.path.ifEmpty { storeDir.toString() })
        val actualStored = if (descriptor.storage == FileStorage.COPY) Path(descriptor.path) else src
        java.io.RandomAccessFile(actualStored.toString(), "rw").use { raf ->
            raf.seek(1_200_000L)
            raf.write(0x00)
            raf.write(0x01)
        }
        void(stored)
        val source = DefaultFilePlaintextSource(descriptors, access, crypto)
        val res = source.read(descriptor.fileId, 0, 2_500_000)
        check(res is FileReadResult.SourceLost) { "expected SourceLost but was $res" }
        assertEquals(1, res.blockIndex)
        assertEquals(
            FileDescriptorStatus.SOURCE_LOST,
            descriptors.findById(descriptor.fileId)?.status,
        )
    }

    @Test
    fun largeFile_servedFrom900MiB_withoutReadingPrefix() = runTest(timeout = 120_000) {
        val db = openMemoryDatabase().database
        val recording = RecordingAccess()
        val work = tempDir("yapyap-plaintext-gib")
        val storeDir = Path(work.toString(), "store")
        val descriptors = DefaultFileDescriptorStore(db)
        // 1 GiB sparse file: only the tail page is written; import still hashes
        // 1 GiB of (mostly zero) bytes through positioned reads.
        val total = 1024L * 1024L * 1024L
        val src = Path(work.toString(), "big.bin")
        val tailAt = total - 4096
        val tail = ByteArray(4096) { (it * 13).toByte() }
        recording.openAppendWriter(src, null).use { w ->
            w.truncate(total)
            // AppendHandle is append-only; write the tail via the platform file.
            java.io.RandomAccessFile(src.toString(), "rw").use { raf ->
                raf.seek(tailAt)
                raf.write(tail)
            }
            w.flushAndSync()
        }
        val blockSize = blockSizeFor(total)
        assertEquals(1024 * 1024, blockSize)
        val store = DefaultFileStore(descriptors, crypto, recording, storeDir, FileServiceConfig(), Clock.System)
        val descriptor = store.import(
            FileImportSource.PathSource(src), "big.bin", "application/octet-stream", keepCopy = false,
        )
        recording.minReadOffset = Long.MAX_VALUE
        recording.readCalls = 0
        val source = DefaultFilePlaintextSource(descriptors, recording, crypto)
        val from = 900L * 1024L * 1024L
        val res = source.read(descriptor.fileId, from, 220 * 1024)
        check(res is FileReadResult.Ok)
        assertEquals(220 * 1024, res.bytes.size)
        assertTrue(res.bytes.all { it == 0.toByte() }, "900 MiB region of the sparse file must be zeros")
        assertTrue(recording.readCalls > 0)
        // Nothing below the containing block's start may have been touched.
        val blockStart = from / blockSize * blockSize
        assertTrue(
            recording.minReadOffset >= blockStart,
            "read prefix below block start: min=${recording.minReadOffset} blockStart=$blockStart",
        )
    }

    private fun void(@Suppress("UNUSED_PARAMETER") vararg ignored: Any?) = Unit
}

150:         while (i < tokens.size && tokens[i] in softKeywords) i++
151:         if (i >= tokens.size || tokens[i] !in hardKeywords) return null
152:         if (tokens[i] == "companion") return "companion"
153:         if (i + 1 >= tokens.size) return null
154:         var j = i + 1
155:         // Skip generic parameter lists (`fun <T> foo`).
156:         while (j < tokens.size && tokens[j].startsWith("<")) j++
157:         if (j >= tokens.size) return null
158:         val raw = tokens[j].trimStart('(', '@')
159:         val name = raw.split('(', '<', ':', '=', ',', ' ').firstOrNull().orEmpty()
160:         if (!name.matches(Regex("[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*"))) return null
161:         return name
162:     }

164:     private fun scan(): List<Violation> {
165:         val violations = mutableListOf<Violation>()
166:         for (root in coreSrcRoots()) {
167:             root.walkTopDown()
168:                 .filter { it.isFile && it.extension == "kt" }
169:                 .forEach { file ->
170:                     var pkg = ""
171:                     // Explicit modifier (or "missing") of the enclosing top-level type-like
172:                     // declaration; null outside member scopes (e.g. inside top-level funs).
173:                     var currentTop: String? = null
174:                     val rel = root.toPath().relativize(file.toPath()).toString()
175:                     file.readLines().forEachIndexed { index, raw ->
176:                         val lineNo = index + 1
177:                         val indent = raw.takeWhile { it == ' ' }.length
178:                         val line = raw.trim().trimStart('﻿')
179:                         if (line.isEmpty() || line.startsWith("//") || line.startsWith("*") ||
180:                             line.startsWith("/*") || line.startsWith("@") ||
181:                             line.startsWith("}") || line.startsWith(")") ||
182:                             line.startsWith("import ") || line.startsWith("package ")
183:                         ) {
184:                             if (line.startsWith("package ")) pkg = line.removePrefix("package ").trim()
185:                             return@forEachIndexed
186:                         }
187:                         val tokens = line.split(Regex("\\s+"))
188:                         if (indent == 0) {
189:                             if (tokens[0] !in visibilityModifiers) {
190:                                 violations += Violation(
191:                                     rel, lineNo, line,
192:                                     "top-level declaration without explicit visibility " +
193:                                             "(mark internal, or whitelist as public)",
194:                                 )
195:                             } else if (tokens[0] == "public") {
196:                                 val name = topLevelName(tokens.drop(1))
197:                                 if (name == null || (name != "companion" && "$pkg.$name" !in publicTopLevelWhitelist)) {
198:                                     violations += Violation(
199:                                         rel, lineNo, line,
200:                                         "public top-level declaration is not on the whitelist " +
201:                                                 "(mark internal, or deliberately list it)",
202:                                     )
203:                                 }
204:                             }
205:                             // Track the enclosing scope: member checks below only apply
206:                             // inside public top-level types (members of internal types
207:                             // are exempt, matching the compiler).
208:                             val headAfterVis = tokens.drop(1).dropWhile { it in softKeywords }.firstOrNull()
209:                             currentTop = if (headAfterVis != null && headAfterVis.trimStart('(') in typeScopeKeywords) {
210:                                 tokens[0].takeIf { it in visibilityModifiers } ?: "missing"
211:                             } else {
212:                                 null
213:                             }
214:                         } else if (indent == 4) {
215:                             if ("override" in tokens) return@forEachIndexed
216:                             if (tokens[0] in visibilityModifiers) return@forEachIndexed
217:                             // Data-class constructor properties (`val x: T,`) carry no
218:                             // modifier by design; see the KDoc gap note.
219:                             if ((tokens[0] == "val" || tokens[0] == "var") && line.endsWith(",")) {
220:                                 return@forEachIndexed
221:                             }
222:                             val head = tokens.dropWhile { it in softKeywords }.firstOrNull()?.trimStart('(')
223:                             if (head != null && head in declarationKeywords && currentTop == "public") {
224:                                 violations += Violation(
225:                                     rel, lineNo, line,
226:                                     "member declaration without explicit visibility",
227:                                 )
228:                             }
229:                         }
230:                         // Deeper indents (locals, nested-type members) are out of scope:
231:                         // the explicit-API compiler warnings still surface them in build output.
232:                     }
233:                 }
234:         }
235:         return violations
236:     }

@Test
    fun largeFile_servedFromHighOffset_withoutReadingPrefix() = runTest {
        val db = openMemoryDatabase().database
        val recording = RecordingAccess()
        val work = tempDir("yapyap-plaintext-gib")
        val storeDir = Path(work.toString(), "store")
        val descriptors = DefaultFileDescriptorStore(db)
        // 128 MiB sparse file (1 MiB blocks, like the 1 GiB case in the plan:
        // both are <= 1024 blocks). Only the tail page is written; import still
        // hashes the logical bytes through positioned reads. A full 1 GiB file
        // would allocate 1 GiB on filesystems without sparse-file support.
        val total = 128L * 1024L * 1024L
        val src = Path(work.toString(), "big.bin")
        val tailAt = total - 4096
        val tail = ByteArray(4096) { (it * 13).toByte() }
        recording.openAppendWriter(src, null).use { w ->
            w.truncate(total)
            java.io.RandomAccessFile(src.toString(), "rw").use { raf ->
                raf.seek(tailAt)
                raf.write(tail)
            }
            w.flushAndSync()
        }
        val blockSize = blockSizeFor(total)
        assertEquals(1024 * 1024, blockSize)
        val store = DefaultFileStore(descriptors, crypto, recording, storeDir, FileServiceConfig(), Clock.System)
        val descriptor = store.import(
            FileImportSource.PathSource(src), "big.bin", "application/octet-stream", keepCopy = false,
        )
        recording.resetCounters()
        val source = DefaultFilePlaintextSource(descriptors, recording, crypto)
        val from = 100L * 1024L * 1024L
        val res = source.read(descriptor.fileId, from, 220 * 1024)
        check(res is FileReadResult.Ok)
        assertEquals(220 * 1024, res.bytes.size)
        assertTrue(res.bytes.all { it == 0.toByte() }, "100 MiB region of the sparse file must be zeros")
        assertTrue(recording.readCalls > 0)
        // Nothing below the containing block's start may have been touched.
        val blockStart = from / blockSize * blockSize
        assertTrue(
            recording.minReadOffset >= blockStart,
            "read read prefix below block start: min=${recording.minReadOffset} blockStart=$blockStart",
        )
    }

Resolving the durability gap by isolating truncate, fsync, free space, and positioned read behind platform-specific calls.

You're right to flag it — the drift is real, but it's smaller than it looks. The facts:

**What design §11 actually requires** (`docs/file/design.md:756-774`):

- Writer stays a **single append position** — staged ranges + drain slicing assume it, so mixed chunkings merge without seeks.
- Only **reads** are positioned (fetch starts at P, §6.6) — "the one exception to pure kotlinx.io".
- Torn appends truncate to P at open; checkpoints fsync once.

**Why the writer grew nio anyway** (`jvmMain/.../io/JvmFileAccess.kt:55-113`):

- `truncate(length)` — `raf.setLength()` (grow sparse + shrink). kotlinx.io `FileSystem` (0.8.1) has no truncate; `ConfigStore`, `JvmAppLogger` only ever use `source`/`sink`/`exists`/`createDirectories`/`delete`. Emulating truncate by copy-to-temp + move would be O(file size) per crash recovery — unacceptable at 100 GB.
- `flushAndSync()` — `channel.force(true)`. kotlinx.io `Sink.flush()` only reaches the OS, not the disk. Without a real fsync, "ACK = durable" (§8) breaks: DB says P advanced, OS crash loses the bytes.
- `freeSpaceBytes()` — explicit reserve check (§8); no kotlinx.io equivalent (`File.usableSpace` / `statvfs` needed).
- `readAt()` — the acknowledged exception (`FileChannel.read` / `pread` until kotlinx-io #241 ships).

So a *pure* kotlinx.io writer can't meet §8 without weakening durability. The good news: the isolation goal is already met — common code never sees nio; it's all behind the `FileAccess` port (`commonMain/.../file/io/FileAccess.kt:35-47`), which also covers the Android content-URI case that `expect`/`actual` couldn't. The "expect/actual" wording in §11 was one implementation of the boundary, not the boundary itself.

**Options:**

1. **Keep append-only contract, document the seam (recommended).** No contract change. Optionally shrink `JvmFileAccess` internals so byte transfer goes through `SystemFileSystem.sink(append=true)` (proven in `JvmAppLogger.kt:90`) and nio/`RandomAccessFile` is only held for `force`/`setLength`/`size` — or just keep it as-is with a comment that nio is an internal detail of the JVM port. iOS then does `open/pread/fsync/ftruncate` behind the same interface. One-line design note in §11 ("realised as `FileAccess` port, not `expect`/`actual`") keeps docs honest.
2. **Pure kotlinx.io, drop fsync+truncate.** Would need redefining ACK to "flushed to OS" and crash recovery by rewrite. Breaks "nothing ACKed is ever lost" and the checkpoint-crash tests. I don't recommend this.
3. **Embrace positioned writes (`writeAt`).** Removes nothing — still needs fsync/truncate/positioned-IO — and destroys the single-append-position invariant the receive engine relies on. Only makes sense with parallel-swarm fetches, which §18 explicitly defers. Don't do this for v1.

My take: the append-only design was correct and is still intact at the interface level — what leaked was an implementation detail inside one JVM file. I'd go with option 1 and leave the contracts (`AppendHandle`, `PositionedHandle`, `FileStore`, `DefaultFilePlaintextSource`) untouched.

How do you want it cleaned up?

- (a) Comment-only: keep `JvmFileAccess` as-is, add a note that nio is JVM-internal and the `FileAccess` port *is* the §11 boundary?
- (b) Minimal-nio refactor: byte transfer via kotlinx.io `sink(append=true)`/`source`, platform handle kept only for `force`/`setLength`/`freeSpace`/`readAt`?
- (c) Something else you had in mind?

content.text: Analyzing current append-only design and evaluating tradeoffs and simplifications if writeAt were available.
Evaluating writeAt for direct offset writes while keeping checkpointed fsync and staging for durability.
Analyzing writeAt to cut double-write IO by tracking coverage in DB and handling concurrent idempotent writes and out-of-order block verification.
Evaluating writeAt crash recovery tradeoffs and concurrency control for sparse file writes.

Speculating freely, no design change: `writeAt` wouldn't unlock concurrent transfers — you already have that. It would just move where the merging happens, and the trade is not clearly a win for v1.

**What you already get without `writeAt`**

The receiver is transfer- and chunking-agnostic by construction (`design.md §8`): every chunk maps to `[index × chunkSize, …)` in its own chunking, lands its byte range, fully-covered ranges are dropped as duplicates. Two transfers with different chunkings already complete one file together, and the gap trigger deliberately cancels nothing — coverage merges whatever arrives. Concurrency is a solved problem logically; the only question is *where the bytes wait* before P advances.

Today they wait in `file_receive_chunks` (`file_id, start_offset, length, plaintext BLOB`), P is the persisted `contiguous_bytes`, and drain is append-only: slice the tail in memory, append what is drainable, one fsync, advance P + delete staged rows in one txn. Crash recovery is trivial — truncate `.part` to P, staged rows drain again, re-hash only the partial block at P. One partial block ever, one fsync per checkpoint.

**What `writeAt` would actually simplify**

- **No double-write.** Today every small-path byte is written twice: once to SQLite as a staged BLOB, once to `.part` at drain. With positioned writes into a preallocated sparse file, you write once and track *coverage* (ranges) in the DB instead of *plaintext*. At 32 MB `maxStagedBytes` that's a real but small saving for ≤10 MB files; it matters more if staging ever grows.
- **No `DEFER` backpressure.** `maxStagedBytes` + silent DEFER exists only because unbounded suffixes behind a stuck gap would pile BLOBs in the DB. With a preallocated sparse file, disk is already reserved, so a racing transfer can write the whole suffix and nobody's memory suffers. The staging bound, the DEFER path in `FileInboundHandler`, and part of the flat-retry rationale in §6.2 could go away.
- **Drain becomes metadata-only.** No DB→file movement; a checkpoint is just "advance P + fsync".

**What it would complicate (the hidden costs)**

- **Out-of-order block verification.** Today P never passes an unverified block and there's exactly one running hasher (the block containing P). With sparse out-of-order writes you'd have many partial blocks at once: per-block incremental hash state, persisted or reconstructed, plus a rule for what "verified" means when bytes arrive non-contiguously. Restart currently re-hashes one partial block from `.part`; with `writeAt` it must re-verify every covered-but-unverified range by re-reading the file, and invalidate ranges whose hashes fail.
- **Crash reconciliation gets harder, not easier.** Today "what was ACKed was durable" holds because staging + P commit in one txn and the file is truncated to P on open. With direct sparse writes, an ACKed coverage row can outlive its bytes (write accepted, fsync at checkpoint never happened, crash). Recovery can't just truncate to P without throwing away verified-but-uncheckpointed bytes, and it can't trust the file without re-hashing. You replace one simple invariant (truncate to P) with range invalidation logic.
- **Concurrency control moves into the file.** SQLite serialises the staged merge for free. Concurrent `pwrite` to one descriptor is safe on JVM (`write(buf, position)` doesn't move the channel position) and via `pwrite` on iOS, but P advancement, fsync, truncate-to-P, and quota/eviction now need explicit coordination around a shared file offset space. At 220 KiB chunks and ≤10 MB files, that's machinery for no new capability.
- **Large files gain nothing.** The fetch path (§6.6) is ordered by construction and already appends at P with no staging — `writeAt` solves a problem that path doesn't have. Swarming (split-by-range parallel fetch from several holders) is the one future that *would* want sparse writes, and it's explicitly deferred (§18).

**Verdict for the speculation**

If `writeAt` existed today, the honest simplification would be: delete `file_receive_chunks` plaintext storage + DEFER, keep a lean received-ranges table, keep P exactly as-is for progress/REQUEST/`PROGRESS` semantics. Everything else — checkpoints, one fsync per checkpoint, P-never-past-unverified-block, pull-backstop timers — stays, because those are durability and protocol properties, not I/O accidents.

I'd keep the append-only design for v1: the double-write cost is bounded and tiny at these sizes, while the crash story stays one line ("truncate to P"). Revisit `writeAt` if either (a) DB BLOB pressure shows up in the soak (§24), or (b) swarming (§18) gets scheduled — that's the feature that actually needs sparse concurrent writes, and by then kotlinx.io #241 may have closed the portability gap anyway.

Want me to sketch what the ranges-table + re-verify-on-restart variant would look like against your current `file_receives` DDL, just as a spike for later?

127:             packetType = PacketType.MESSAGE,
128:             dispositionRequested = true,
129:             createdAt = now,

131:             source = ctx.localDeviceId,

156:             tag = OutboxTag(OutboxTag.Kind.MESSAGE, payload.messageId),

776: ## 12. Layering and data ownership
777: 
778: **Two grains, one seam:**
779: 
780: - **Routing owns the `transferId` grain** — device vocabulary: the per-device fan-out, per-transfer chunk
781:   parameters, per-depot resume points (the pusher's state, restart-recoverable from its rows plus the
782:   outbox), the incoming-transfer rows, chunk encryption and decryption, sealed-half protection and every transfer key,
783:   **all
784:   transfer signaling** — OFFER, CHUNK, ACK, COMPLETE and CANCEL travel between the two devices that
785:   participate in the transfer — the relay store, and the request attempts. For large files it owns the fetch
786:   channel (§6.6): opening the session and the channel, the frames, the credit window — device and channel
787:   vocabulary, with no table.
788: - **The orchestrator owns the `fileId`/account grain** — file vocabulary: send rows per (file, peer account),
789:   receive state per `fileId` (coverage, checkpoints, block verification), serve rows per (file, requester
790:   account), the serve gate, the accept/decline verdicts (including the large-file auto-download decision),
791:   the store's copies and references, and the REQUEST trigger. It never holds a key. It sees account-level events through
792:   the `FileCarrier` port and issues
793:   account-level ops; source devices may appear in events as *facts* (like "re-verify messages from a
794:   device"), never as *addresses* — replies are routing-owned signaling.
795: 
796: The precedent is the message path: the router fans out per device and the orchestrator never addresses one;
797: files push the same line one step further (transfer state itself is device-grain, so it lives routing-side).
798: A headless relay node's orchestrator (file service, REQUEST logic, GUI progress) is completely uninvolved in
799: forwarding. Serve-on-REQUEST is the one relay-node case that *is* orchestrator business (we hold the file →
800: own traffic → our row, account-grain, pushed through the same machinery).

Good pointers — I've checked the bootstrap pattern against the file path. Here's how I'd map it, plus my take on the send path.

**Keys, bootstrap-style.** `BootstrapProtection` threads the external secret explicitly on the protect side (`protect(payload, source, target, createdAt, sharedSecret?)`, `DefaultEnvelopeProtectionService.protectBootstrap(..., sharedSecret)`) and resolves it internally on the open side via `BootstrapKeySource` (`protection/envelope/BootstrapProtection.kt:28,41-66,98-103,150-152`). The faithful file analogue:
- `encryptChunk(transferId, chunkIndex, key, plaintext)` / `sealOffer(sealedBytes, target)` take the key (or session peer) explicitly — the pusher owns its `file_pushes` row and passes its key per call, protection stores nothing.
- `decryptChunk` / `openOffer` resolve per open: sealed half via the ratchet session manager (like messages), chunk key via a small `FileTransferKeySource` (transferId → key) declared in `protection`, implemented by the routing incoming-transfer store. Mirror of `BootstrapKeySource`.
- Honest alternative: pass the key explicitly on *both* sides (the inbound handler already loads the row for chunking/fileId mapping, so the key is free). Fewer moving parts, equally stateless. My preference is explicit-both unless you want the strict bootstrap mirror — tell me which.

**Send path — I agree with you.** Two publish paths would rot: `DefaultMessagingService.sendMessage` (`orchestrator/runtime/message/DefaultMessagingService.kt:260-359`) already owns room refusal checks (REMOVED), size guards, DAG append, member fan-out, and per-member reports. A parallel `FileTransferService.send` reimplementing that is the worst option. I'd do:
- All outbound composition lives in `MessagingService`: new `sendFile(roomId, text, source, fileName, mimeType, keepCopy)` that uses `FileService` for import/descriptor/classify (`SMALL_FILE_MAX_BYTES`), appends the message with attachments through the existing `dagEngine.append` path, then starts per-device push via `FileCarrier` for small files.
- `orchestrator/file` keeps storage truth: descriptors, I/O, receive engine, plaintext source, serve gate. No publish logic.
- `orchestrator/runtime/file` keeps the file GUI facade for step 23 (progress/accept/decline/open/cancel) — and its `sendFile`, if the GUI contract wants one entry point, becomes a thin delegate to `MessagingService.sendFile` rather than a second implementation. Exact facade split gets nailed in step 23's `gui-api.md`, but no logic is duplicated either way.

**Events + e2e.** Noted: full `FileCarrier` events now (account-level only — progress in/out, ready, failed; no device addresses across the seam), everything wired in `NodeGraph`, live-Tor proof deferred for this machine — e2e via the recording-transport two-router pattern (`DefaultRouterE2eeIntegrationTest`-style) plus engine tests.

answers: Here I don't really want a separate function sendFile which sends a message, that is confusing. We shouldn't have a separate sendFile in the fileservice either. I'm not sure what would be the best way to do it, but we have the Message object, maybe we could add the file descriptors there and if they are there, the messaging service would append them? That gets messy, though with the gui having to generate the descriptors separately and when does the file push actually start, from the messaging service? That mixes concerns a bit, but it doesn't make sense for the gui to call (and maybe forget) to execute a separate method here. Extending the message schema with picked-file inputs and staging async import before DAG append.

Locked in — here's the final Phase C shape as I understand it, ready for your go-ahead:

**Keys: explicit both sides.** `encryptChunk(transferId, chunkIndex, key, plaintext)` / `decryptChunk(transferId, chunkIndex, key, chunk)` — the pusher passes its `file_pushes` row key, the inbound handler passes its `file_incoming_transfers` row key after the row lookup it already needs for fileId/chunking. Sealed OFFER/REQUEST halves go through the ratchet session manager like messages; every FILE envelope signed like messages. No key storage in protection, no new key-source port.

**Send: one path, owned by `MessagingService`.** No `sendFile` anywhere — I agree that name lies about what's happening. Concretely:
- `Message` (the GUI-facing send input in `orchestrator/runtime/message/MessagingTypes.kt`) gains the picked files alongside text — e.g. `pickedFiles: List<PickedFile(source, fileName, mimeType, keepCopy)>` — while the existing `attachments` stay as the already-resolved references.
- `MessagingService.sendMessage` becomes the complete I/O for all messages: it imports each picked file through `FileService` (descriptor + `fileId`), classifies by `SMALL_FILE_MAX_BYTES`, appends the DAG draft with the resulting attachments through the existing `dagEngine.append` path (same refusal checks, same per-member fan-out), then starts the per-device push via `FileCarrier` for small files. The GUI can never forget a second call because there isn't one.
- For Phase C this suspends through import (small files hash fast); the "preparing" async publish for minute-long 100 GB hashes is a Phase F/step-23 concern, noted but not built now.
- `orchestrator/file` keeps descriptors, store, receive engine, plaintext source, serve gate — no publish logic. The `runtime/file` facade keeps progress/accept/decline/open/cancel (step 23 contract), with sending flowing through messaging.

**Everything else per plan:** `FileIngestPort` with `checkOffer` + `ingest`; `FileCarrier` on `Router` with `pushFile`/`cancelFile` + router-owned COMPLETE fan-out, foreign targets DECLINED; `FileCarrier` events minimal four (outgoing/incoming progress, ready, failed, account-level only); `RouterConfig` gains `fileTransferTtl = 2.days`, `maxInFlightChunks = 16`, `fileChunkRetryDelay = 10s`; `OutboxOutcome` gains `packetId`, `OutboxTag.Kind.FILE`, blob-less due query with non-FILE first; `file_pushes`/`file_incoming_transfers`/`file_receives`/`file_receive_chunks`/`file_transfers` each with own migration (8–11); `FileLimits` chunk derivation in `wiring`; everything wired in `NodeGraph`; e2e via recording-transport two-router tests plus engine tests, live-Tor proof deferred.

Analyzing the messaging flow and identifying that attachments are sent as metadata only with no file import or byte transfer implemented.

Today the attachment path is **metadata-only and effectively unwired** — here's the exact walk for "image + text":

**1. GUI side — attachments can't be produced.**
`ChatController.send` (`composeApp/.../gui/state/ChatController.kt:122-138`) calls `runtime.messaging.sendMessage(roomId, Message(body))` — text only, no attachments. The send input `Message` (`core/.../orchestrator/runtime/message/MessagingTypes.kt:39-42`) *does* have `attachments: List<MessageAttachment>`, where each `MessageAttachment` (`:44-49`) is `fileId, fileName, mimeType, totalBytes`. But a picked image has no `fileId` yet — the `fileId` is a block-hash over the bytes (`FileIds`, Phase A) produced by `FileStore.import`. So the GUI would have to import first — and it can't: `FileStore`/`FileService` exist from Phase B but are **not wired anywhere** (no matches in `wiring/`; nothing in `NodeGraph` constructs them). The GUI capability flag confirms it: `attachments: Boolean = false` (`composeApp/.../gui/capabilities/Capabilities.kt:22`).

**2. If the GUI faked the metadata, the message would still send — with no bytes behind it.**
`DefaultMessagingService.sendMessage` (`core/.../orchestrator/runtime/message/DefaultMessagingService.kt:260-359`) maps each `MessageAttachment` to a wire `MessagePayload.Attachment` (`:295-302`), appends the DAG draft with text + attachments (`:303`), notifies windows, and fans out per room member via `router.sendMessage` (`:337-344`). That part works — the attachment rides the DAG message as a notification ("you may want this file"), which is exactly the design's message/transfer split. But nothing imports or hashes the file, nothing classifies small vs large, and **no transfer starts**: there is no pusher yet (Phase C step 13), no `FileProtection` (still `PlaintextFileProtection`), no receive engine (step 12), no REQUEST/pull path.

**3. Receiving renders the label, never the bytes.**
The message would display as `MessageDisplayItem.File(fileId, fileName, fileSize)` (`MessagingTypes.kt:22-29`), but no OFFER/CHUNK ever arrives, no `.part` is assembled, and no REQUEST can pull the bytes (serve gate + `FilePlaintextSource` consumers land in Phase C/D).

**What changes with the agreed Phase C shape:** the GUI goes back to one call — `sendMessage(roomId, Message(text, pickedFiles))` with the raw picked image (path/URI + name + mime + keepCopy). `MessagingService` does the rest: import via `FileService` (hash → `fileId` + descriptor), append the DAG message with the resulting attachments, and for small files start the per-device push through `FileCarrier`. The GUI never touches descriptors or transfer calls, so there's nothing to forget — which was your exact concern.

Detailing the end-to-end attachment send path and wire protocol for the agreed design.

With the agreed design, the GUI makes **one call** and everything else is backend choreography. Taking "image + caption text" as the example:

**1. GUI: single `sendMessage`.**
```kotlin
messaging.sendMessage(roomId, Message(
  content = "look at this",
  pickedFiles = [PickedFile(source = <image path/URI>, fileName = "img.jpg",
                             mimeType = "image/jpeg", keepCopy = true)]
))
```
No `fileId`, no descriptor, no second "now push it" call — nothing to forget. The existing text validations (removed-member, size) run as today (`DefaultMessagingService.kt:260-292`).

**2. `MessagingService.sendMessage`: import → append → trigger push.**
- For each picked file it calls `FileService.import`: copy into `files/store/` (keepCopy) or reference in place, hashing in the same pass → descriptor with `fileId` + block list; classifies by `SMALL_FILE_MAX_BYTES` (10 MB). An image is small.
- Builds the wire attachments (`fileId, fileName, mimeType, totalBytes`) and appends the DAG draft exactly like today (`:294-303`) — the message stays a notification, carrying no key and no bytes.
- Existing per-member text fan-out runs unchanged (`:337-344`). Additionally, for each small attachment it calls `FileCarrier.pushFile(fileId, memberAccount)`. Large files stop here (no push — Phase F).

**3. Pusher (routing, per device).** Each `pushFile` fans out to that account's devices (the `OutboundMessenger` pattern): one transfer per device with its own `transferId`, snapshotted chunk size from `FileLimits`, fresh `randomBytes` key held in its `file_pushes` row (migration 10). The OFFER marker goes through the outbox (`OutboxTag.Kind.FILE`, id = `transferId`, TTL `fileTransferTtl = 2d`): public half (chunk size, total, start index) in clear for relays, sealed half (`fileId`, block list, key, name, mime) ratchet-encrypted to the target. On OFFER-ACK the engine streams CHUNK rows in a `maxInFlightChunks = 16` window, each chunk AEAD'd with AAD (`transferId`, `chunkIndex`) under the transfer key and signed; retries are flat at `fileChunkRetryDelay = 10s`. Target-DECLINED on the OFFER is terminal; any other terminal NACK ends the transfer as ENDED; COMPLETE resolves COMPLETED.

**4. Receiver.** `FileInboundHandler`: OFFER → open sealed half, `checkOffer` via `FileIngestPort` (block list vs `fileId`, free-space reserve, READY check) → create `file_incoming_transfers` row → ACK (an already-READY file gets ACK + COMPLETE, never DECLINED). CHUNK → look up row by `transferId` (unknown → DECLINED, never stored), decrypt with the row's key (explicit-both-sides, per your call), hand `(fileId, offset, plaintext)` to the ingest port → Staged / Duplicate / silent DEFER. The receive engine merges byte coverage across transfers and chunkings, checkpoints every 8 MB / 2 s (append, one fsync, one P commit), never advances P past an unverified block. On full coverage + verified blocks: atomic rename → READY, then COMPLETE to every live author through `FileCarrier` (router fans out from its incoming rows).

**5. What the GUI observes.** The agreed four account-level `FileCarrier` events — outgoing progress, incoming progress, ready, failed — plus the message itself rendering first with its attachment label while bytes land. Cancel flows through `FileCarrier.cancelFile`; a declined OFFER surfaces as refused, never auto-resurrected.

So the GUI's mental model stays "messages, some with attachments" — picking a file just adds an entry to the send input, and the backend turns it into DAG-notify + transfer machinery without a second API.

Analyzing toDisplayItem logic and noting attachments are unimplemented, requiring Phase C/GUI mapping via fileService.

Yes — with one precision on naming: on the **send** side it's picked files (raw input), on the **display** side it's attachment references. The flow you're describing is exactly the design:

- A received (or own, just-sent) message arrives as display items: the text plus one item per attachment carrying `fileId, fileName, fileSize` — that's today's `MessageDisplayItem.File` shape (`MessagingTypes.kt:22-29`). One gap to be honest about: `toDisplayItem()` currently renders only the text and drops attachments (`DefaultMessagingService.kt:459-469` never produces `File` items) — wiring attachments into display items is part of the Phase C/GUI work, not something that works today.
- For each attachment the GUI asks the file facade — `FileTransferService` in `orchestrator/runtime/file` — "give me this image": path to render when the file is READY in the permanent store, progress placeholder while it's incoming (driven by the agreed incoming-progress events), accept/open for large files above auto-download. The orchestrator vends paths and metadata; the GUI never touches the store directly (design §10).
- So the GUI's read model stays: message object in, attachment references out, file bytes via one file-service call per `fileId` — symmetric to the send side being one `sendMessage` call with picked files.

31:  *

37:  * short lifetime (`syncAttemptTimeout`), and its outcome comes back through [onAttemptOutcome]:

44: internal class SyncRetryProcessor(
45:     private val ctx: RoutingContext,
46:     private val attempts: SyncAttemptStore,
47:     private val syncs: SyncPayloadProvider,
48:     private val systemSender: SystemSender,
49:     private val outboxProcessor: OutboxProcessor,
50:     private val peerPolicy: SyncPeerPolicy,
51:     maxIdlePoll: StateFlow<Duration>,
52:     /** No candidate has an open link: whoever keeps links open may want to try these now. */
53:     private val onNoLink: suspend (PeerId) -> Unit = {},
54: ) {
55:     /**
56:      * Devices whose attempt for a sync went unanswered (expired, or a NACK that isn't a
57:      * decline), asked again only after the other candidates. In memory: a restart forgets it,

59:      */
60:     private val unanswered = HashMap<Uuid, MutableSet<PeerId>>()

63:     private val retryLoop = RetryLoop(
64:         earliestPendingRetryAt = { attempts.earliestDueAt() },

66:         processDue = { processDue() },
67:         maxIdlePoll = maxIdlePoll,
68:         onProcessFailed = { error ->

72:                 message = "Sync retry processing failed",

75:         },

83:     }

86:         retryLoop.notifyChanged()
87:     }
88: 
89:     /** Starts asking for [syncId] (idempotent). */

91:         attempts.start(syncId, firstAttemptAt)
92:         wake()
93:     }
94: 
95:     /**
96:      * [account] asserts it can serve [syncId] after all. When every candidate device has
97:      * declined (the sync is inert), its devices may be asked again; mid-round rotation is
98:      * left alone, so one candidate cannot hog the requests while others never get a turn.
99:      */
100:     suspend fun reopen(syncId: Uuid, account: AccountId) {
101:         val declined = attempts.declinedDevices(syncId)
102:         if (declined.isEmpty()) return
103:         val candidates = candidateDevices(syncs.syncCandidates(syncId))
104:         if (candidates.any { it !in declined }) return
105:         attempts.removeDeclined(syncId, ctx.devices.getAllPeerDevicesForAccount(account))
106:         attempts.advanceToNow(listOf(syncId), ctx.clock.now())
107:         wake()
108:     }
